folios.label: Capability / invention
folios.question: Can AI do whole tasks, and reliably?

rows.line: The length of task AI can finish keeps doubling about every four months.
rows.who: AI Futures Project (Kokotajlo, Lifland, Jurkovic et al.)

rows.line: François Chollet argued that an intelligence explosion cannot happen, and that the first superhuman AI would be just another step in steady, roughly linear progress.
Models still cannot learn on the job the way people do, and it holds them back.
Ajeya Cotra's median for the longest METR fifty-percent time horizon reported by the end of 2026 was about twenty-four hours of expert work.
Gwern argued that once a scalable architecture exists, simply training ever bigger neural networks will keep yielding more sophisticated general abilities without fundamentally new designs.
Robin Hanson put less than one chance in a hundred on a single hand-coded AI leaping, without warning, from near impotence to overwhelming power.
Gary Marcus bet Miles Brundage that by the end of 2027 AI will still fail at least three of ten demanding tasks, from understanding films to Nobel-level discovery.
Hans Moravec projected that cheap computers would match the brain's processing power before 2030, bringing hardware suited to humanlike robots in the 2020s.
Each test AI passes shows the test's limits, not that AI has arrived.
Data-centre buildings and their power hookups are the bottleneck.
If the trend speeds up, by March 2027 AI could reliably do software tasks that take people years.
rows.who: AI Futures Project (Kokotajlo, Lifland, Jurkovic et al.)

rows.line: The AI 2027 scenario has AI that automates AI research in early 2027 compounding into artificial superintelligence before that year is out.
The AI 2027 scenario had AI assistants speeding the leading lab's algorithmic progress by about half again by early 2026.
Models might do most of a software engineer's work end to end within six to twelve months.
I. J. Good judged it more likely than not that a machine surpassing every human intellect would be built within the twentieth century, setting off an intelligence explosion.
Ray Kurzweil projected that around 2023 a thousand dollars of computer hardware would buy raw processing equal to his own estimate for one human brain.
Ray Kurzweil forecast that before 2030 the combined thinking capacity of non-biological intelligence would exceed that of all human brains put together.

Ray Solomonoff expected a general theory of AI most likely within two to twenty-five years, and a machine with human-level problem-solving in its designed fields perhaps as little as a decade or so later.
Whole projects stay far behind single skills, with the best score on real freelance projects below [test:frontier_uneven].
rows.settles: The best model completing most of the Remote Labor Index's projects.

rows.line: The length of the software tasks AI can finish keeps doubling at least as fast as the scenario assumes, every [test:horizon_fast] or less.
rows.settles: The doubling time lengthening beyond what the scenario assumes.

rows.line: The agents Princeton's tracker tests grow more dependable far more slowly than they grow more accurate.
rows.settles: Reliability rising as fast as accuracy across the next models the tracker tests.

rows.line: AI speeds up its own invention
rows.settles: AI starts speeding up its own invention if independent tests show agents doing more than a day of research work for each day a person puts in, and needing a person's help on long tasks less than half the time.

rows.line: The race ending of AI 2027 has special economic zones filling with robot factories from 2028, with a robot economy covering them by early 2030.
An AI that codes better than the best people arrives in 2027.
The AI 2027 scenario placed a superhuman AI researcher, one that outdoes the best people at AI research, at around September 2027.
Scott Alexander puts his chance of AI doom at about one in five, the lowest estimate among the authors of AI 2027.
Sam Altman told TIME that OpenAI would have an internal system he would call AGI before the end of 2026, while conceding it was not there yet.
Sam Altman wrote that 2026 would likely bring AI systems able to work out genuinely new insights.
Sam Altman said 2027 may bring robots able to carry out tasks in the real world.
Sam Altman wrote that superintelligence might arrive within a few thousand days, though it could take longer, and said he is confident it will come.
If scaling continues, AI as able as a country of geniuses arrives within a year or two.
Dario Amodei put nine chances in ten on datacentre AI equal to a whole nation of top experts arriving within a decade, through a soft but steep takeoff.
Leopold Aschenbrenner called it strikingly plausible that models could do the job of the engineers and researchers who build AI by 2027.
Leopold Aschenbrenner expects that in 2027 or 2028 models will be as capable as the leading experts and work much like a drop-in remote employee.
Leopold Aschenbrenner expected automated AI research to produce superintelligence, vastly smarter than people, before this decade is out.
Tamay Besiroglu places full replacement of remote workers by AI about five years ahead of Ege Erdil's date, which puts it near 2040.
Nick Bostrom judged it unlikely that the climb from human-level AI to superintelligence would take decades, and more likely that it would be fast or moderate.
Nick Bostrom clarified that, all things considered, he gave less than even odds that superintelligence would be developed by 2033.
Joe Carlsmith gave about two chances in three that advanced, agentic, strategically aware AI becomes possible and affordable to build by 2070.
Joe Carlsmith raised his estimate that power-seeking AI causes an existential catastrophe by 2070 from about one in twenty to more than one in ten.
David Chalmers put his credence in human-level AI before 2100 at more than one half, while saying he would be surprised to see it within the next thirty years.
Paul Christiano put about one chance in seven on AI able to build a Dyson sphere by 2030, and about two chances in five by 2040.
Paul Christiano gave even odds on whether an intelligence explosion driven by software improvements alone is possible at all.
Paul Christiano expected that, without solving intent alignment, AI failure would come as a gradual loss of human steering to optimised proxies, possibly ending in a sudden cascade.

Ajeya Cotra's biological anchors report modelled a median in the early 2050s for transformative AI, which she rounded to about 2050, with most aggressive and most conservative plausible medians of 2040 and 2080.
Ajeya Cotra gave about one chance in ten that AI fully automates AI research and development, matching human researchers, by the end of 2026.
Andrew Critch put about even odds, on top of other risks, on humanity gradually handing the planet to AI after it is built, mostly during the 2030s, with the last humans gone by 2050.
Tom Davidson's takeoff model put a median of 2043 on AI able to readily automate all cognitive work, with about one chance in ten by 2030 and four in five by 2070.
Tom Davidson's best guess is that AI goes from matching human professionals at almost all cognitive work to far surpassing them in less than a year.
Ege Erdil and Tamay Besiroglu doubt that AI improving its own software alone will set off an intelligence explosion, holding that compute and experiments bound progress.
Ege Erdil expects AI able to replace a remote worker at essentially every task to arrive around 2045.
Extrapolating past progress in AI subfields, Robin Hanson estimated that broadly human-level AI without brain emulation would take more than two to four centuries.
Demis Hassabis expects AGI around 2030, give or take a year, and says that looking back people will see we are already on the lower slopes of the singularity.
Holden Karnofsky gave better than one chance in ten of transformative AI by 2036, about even odds by 2060, and around two chances in three by 2100.
Daniel Kokotajlo's August 2026 median for artificial superintelligence is March 2029, a few months after his median for AI that beats top experts.
Daniel Kokotajlo's August 2026 median for an automated coder, an AI that labs would rather keep than their human coders, is November 2027.
Daniel Kokotajlo puts his chance of catastrophe from AI at around seven in ten, a figure he calls infamously high.
Daniel Kokotajlo's August 2026 median for AI that matches or exceeds the best human experts on almost every cognitive task is November 2028.
Jan Kulveit and co-authors argue that if AI keeps displacing human labour, thought and consent across economy, culture and state, humans will probably lose effective control without any takeover.
Ray Kurzweil set 2045 as the year of the Singularity, when machine intelligence created by people would vastly exceed all human intelligence combined.
Ray Kurzweil bet publicly that a machine would pass a rigorous Turing test, judged under formal rules with expert interrogators, by 2029.
Yann LeCun says language models will not reach human-level intelligence, and that within five years we may at best know we are on the right path.
Eli Lifland's August 2026 median for artificial superintelligence is July 2033, about a year after his median for AI that beats top experts.
Eli Lifland's August 2026 median for an automated coder, an AI that labs would rather keep than their human coders, is January 2030.
Eli Lifland's August 2026 median for AI that matches or exceeds the best human experts on almost every cognitive task is July 2032.
William MacAskill and Fin Moorhouse think it fairly likely that AI matches human research labour within two decades, and possibly well within one.
William MacAskill and Fin Moorhouse give roughly even odds that AI improving its own software sets off accelerating growth in AI capability.
Hans Moravec expected machines to overtake people even in walking, manual dexterity and social skills within about fifty years of 1998.
AI improving itself cannot get past limits that sit outside the lab.
Stephen Omohundro argued that any sufficiently advanced goal-seeking AI, unless deliberately designed otherwise, will resist being shut down, copy itself and acquire resources.
OpenAI builds an automated AI researcher by March 2028.
OpenAI has an automated AI research intern by September 2026.
Toby Ord estimated about one chance in ten that unaligned AI causes an existential catastrophe within the next hundred years, the largest single risk he assessed.
Stuart Russell said superintelligent AI would probably arrive within his children's lifetimes, barring catastrophe, while calling it quite unlikely in the next few years.
Carl Shulman puts the chance that AI takes control of humanity's future at between a fifth and a quarter, depending on the day.
Carl Shulman expects that once AI directs a converted industrial base, the robot population will double in under a year, and then within months.
Mustafa Suleyman predicted an AI could turn a modest stake into a million dollars selling online, with light human help within a year and probably entirely on its own within three to five years.
Vernor Vinge expected humans to have the means to create superhuman intelligence within about three decades, and said he would be surprised if it came before 2005 or after 2030.
Eliezer Yudkowsky argued that an AI improving itself would most likely either stall or take off explosively, since a gradual, human-paced takeoff would need implausibly precise diminishing returns.
The young Eliezer Yudkowsky cited 2035 as the most widely quoted date for the Singularity and said he, like many others, expected it substantially sooner.
Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares hold that if anyone builds artificial superintelligence with anything like today's methods and understanding, everyone on Earth will die.
Memory and chip packaging are short.
With many agents working on a task at once, most valuable office work comes to turn on the cost of computing and the systems around it, not on whether models are good enough.
rows.settles: Valuable office tasks staying out of AI's reach even where computing is cheap.

rows.line: Labs and companies keep paying more for the steps models cannot yet take, even as each new model takes more of them on its own.
rows.settles: What labs and companies pay for practice work and for fitting models falling as the models improve.

rows.line: Better data, more than better model designs, drives how much a model learns from its training, so progress comes to rest on finding new data.
rows.settles: Design changes, not data, turning out to carry the gains at the largest scale.

rows.line: Research speeds up far more in software and mathematics than in drug development, materials or physics, where the slowest steps are experiments.
rows.settles: A broad speed-up in the experiment-heavy sciences at the same time as in software.

rows.line: Data centres arrive faster and with less warning than the grid's planners assume, so getting connected holds back new American sites.
rows.settles: New sites being connected to the grid as fast as they are built.

rows.line: AI's help with AI research brings steady gains, not accelerating ones.
rows.settles: Each new model's gains on AI research tasks coming faster than the last's, with nothing lost along the way.

rows.line: Chinese labs do not take the lead at the frontier while the best chips, the tests that matter and the paying customers stay American.
rows.settles: A Chinese lab's model becoming the best at the frontier.

rows.line: Training for long work whose results are hard to check, in fields such as biology, security and matters of taste, comes to rest on records of real work inside firms, because tasks staged by contractors stop teaching models.
rows.settles: Staged practice tasks going on improving models at long office work.

rows.line: As the scenario is written, AI completes most real, paid freelance projects end to end by the end of 2027.
Too few electricians, welders and other tradespeople hold back the building of data centres, so the largest technology firms keep paying to train them.
rows.settles: Data-centre projects facing no delays tied to shortages of skilled trades.

folios.label: Innovation: products and applications
folios.question: What gets built on it, and who sells it?

rows.line: Practice tasks with automatic graders, and the expert-written data they consume, are where the shortage goes next.
Checking AI's work is sold as a category of its own.
rows.settles: No independent category forming, the checks staying inside the labs' and clouds' own platforms.
rows.who: This site, extending Gillian Hadfield and Andrew Koh

rows.line: Insurers write AI's mistakes out of their standard policies, so the cover has to be bought and priced on its own.
rows.settles: Standard policies going on covering AI's mistakes at no extra price.
rows.who: This site, extending Gillian Hadfield and Andrew Koh

rows.line: Proof of what an AI agent (a model that carries out tasks with software tools on a person's behalf) did, and who answers for it, becomes a bottleneck once agents handle money.
Large platforms move to keep outside agents off them more often than they let them in.
rows.settles: Platforms opening to outside agents more often than they block them, counted under one rule for both; this site's hand-kept ledger does not yet sweep both sides that way, so it tests nothing yet.
rows.who: Byrne Hobart and Nikhil Davar and Soren Larson

rows.line: Labs spend more each year with the firms that sell practice tasks, graders and expert data.
rows.settles: That spending falling once each firm counted a year ago has reported again; the hand-kept tally of disclosed deals is too thin to test it yet.

rows.line: Start-ups that build a model for one field fall behind as the labs' general models improve, outside a few regulated niches where data is scarce.
rows.settles: Models built for one field keeping their lead over each new general release.

rows.line: Firms outside the labs become large buyers of training data and practice tasks, so the labs stop being almost the only customers.
rows.settles: The labs remaining almost all of the spending on training data and practice tasks.

rows.line: Insurers sell cover written for AI's mistakes, not only exclusions from standard policies.
rows.settles: AI cover staying a niche product that large buyers do not purchase.

rows.line: A formal pause looks unlikely; instead the biggest labs, loosely in step, slow the public release of their most powerful models.
rows.settles: Labs releasing their best models to the public as soon as they are trained.

rows.line: If training a model further on a firm's own work keeps getting cheaper, apps train their own instead of renting the best.
rows.settles: Apps built on open models still paying labs' prices because training their own stays too costly.

rows.line: Leading firms that host models, sell training data or do custom training, such as Baseten, Mercor and Applied Compute, converge on one business, tuning open models for firms and selling them the use.
rows.settles: These firms staying in separate businesses.

rows.line: The first large failure of a market run by AI agents comes from no one being able to check what an agent did, not from agents lacking skill.
rows.settles: The first large agent failure traced to agents that could not do the work.
rows.who: This site, extending Gillian Hadfield and Andrew Koh

folios.label: Diffusion: early adoption
folios.question: How fast do firms and people take it up?

rows.line: AI's big economic effects arrive over decades, not years.
Adoption stays slow wherever mistakes are costly.
In the jobs most exposed to AI, workers in their early twenties fall behind workers over fifty [cite:canaries], while in the least exposed jobs they do not.
rows.settles: The same gap opening in the least exposed jobs.

rows.line: AI is not an ordinary technology
rows.settles: AI stops looking like an ordinary technology if three things happen together. Models become nearly as reliable on long jobs as on short ones, and not just because the tests have run out of longer tasks. Most of the labour-market trackers we follow break at the same time. And either the share of work hours done with AI passes a fifth, or productivity runs well above trend for years on end.

rows.line: The share of American firms using AI stays within the pace this site calls normal, below [test:firms_normal].
rows.settles: The share of firms using AI climbing past that pace.

rows.line: No single leap in ability unlocks AI's economic value.
Engineers who fit AI into each customer's own work stay scarce, so their pay rises or employers settle for weaker hires.
rows.settles: These roles becoming easy to fill, and their pay premium fading.

rows.line: Labs keep buying the consultancies that put AI to work inside companies, to get their staff faster than hiring allows.
rows.settles: Labs building these teams by hiring and buying no such firms.

rows.line: Agents take hold first in job search, property and other matching markets.
rows.settles: Agents spreading first in markets where people rarely hire human agents.

rows.line: AI does not wipe out software engineering jobs, and demand for engineers may rise as software gets cheaper to make.
rows.settles: Software engineering employment falling as AI coding tools spread.

rows.line: Firms increasingly buy AI's work through a party with assets and a licence that can be held liable, such as an established service firm.
rows.settles: Buyers taking AI's work on long, unpredictable tasks from parties that cannot answer for its mistakes.

rows.line: Official output statistics miss most of AI's gains, which come as better quality and saved time that no price records.
rows.settles: Official statistics capturing AI's gains in quality and saved time as use spreads.
rows.who: Diane Coyle and John Lourenze Poquiz

folios.label: Diffusion: adaptation
folios.question: What happens to work, pay and output as firms reorganise?

rows.line: Tyler Cowen guesses AI will raise annual economic growth by only about half a percentage point, because slow-moving sectors such as government, health and education act as bottlenecks.
Workers stop sharing the gains
rows.settles: The case that workers share in AI's gains fails if the typical full-time worker's pay, after inflation, sits below its level at the end of 2022, just before ChatGPT, for four quarters running while the economy's output keeps growing. Pascual Restrepo, an economist who models work once machines can do every task, finds that workers' total pay never falls below its level before such AI unless something else, such as market power over computing, gets in the way; the typical worker's pay is the nearest measure this site reads.

rows.line: Robin Hanson cited his historical-trend projection, whose median put a switch to world output doubling every year or two at about 2025.
Ray Kurzweil expects the most diligent people to reach longevity escape velocity around 2030, gaining more than a year of life expectancy for every year that passes.
Ray Kurzweil expected robots the size of blood cells to be workable by around 2030, with scanning the living brain from the inside among their leading uses.
In no quarter before 2034 does American real output per person stand [test:no_growth_jump] or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before.
rows.settles: A quarter before 2034 that clears the bet's line.
rows.who: Benjamin Moll, Alex Imas and five others

rows.line: The AI 2027 scenario expects AI to be doing a quarter of the remote jobs of 2024 by October 2027, with unemployment about a point higher than a year before.
Dario Amodei predicts that once powerful AI exists, biology and medicine will fit the coming half-century to century of progress into five to ten years.
Tamay Besiroglu expects explosive economic growth, above thirty percent a year, once AI can flexibly stand in for human workers.
Paul Christiano put about three chances in ten on a fast takeoff, expecting world output to finish a doubling over four years before any single-year doubling begins.

Experts surveyed by Ezra Karger and colleagues expect that if AI outperforms humans on many tasks by 2030, US growth would rise to around four percent a year, against about two and a half percent in their overall forecast.
rows.who: Ezra Karger and colleagues (Forecasting Research Institute)

rows.line: Robin Hanson guessed that brain emulations would be the first machines able to replace human workers wholesale, arriving within about a century and then driving monthly economic doublings.
Robin Hanson's growth model implied that once machines can stand in for most human labour, world output would grow about ten times faster, doubling roughly every eighteen months.
Robin Hanson argued that if brain uploads arrive before other human-level AI, cheap copying would multiply them and push wages toward subsistence even as total wealth grows.
The economists' scenarios only pull apart after 2027.
rows.who: Korinek et al. (The Anthropic Institute, WP 2026-02)

rows.line: Extreme case: growth soars and workers' share of income falls sharply.
rows.who: Korinek et al. (The Anthropic Institute, WP 2026-02)

rows.line: Modest case: AI adds under half a point a year to growth by 2030.
rows.who: Korinek, Jones, Sacher, Cotter and McCrory (The Anthropic Institute, WP 2026-02)

rows.line: Substantial case: output rises and some office jobs go by 2030.
rows.who: Korinek et al. (The Anthropic Institute, WP 2026-02)

rows.line: Ray Kurzweil predicts that during the 2030s nanobots will link the upper layers of the neocortex to the cloud, directly extending human thinking.
William MacAskill and Fin Moorhouse think it more likely than not that, once AI matches human researchers, a hundred years of technological progress follows in under a decade.

Anders Sandberg and Nick Bostrom concluded that, if electrophysiological-level models suffice, emulating a whole human brain should become feasible before 2050, with simple mammals ten to twenty years earlier.
Phil Trammell argues that limits on splitting research across many AI workers could delay a technological singularity, though automating research would probably still produce an explosion.
As AI takes over paid work, governments move tax from wages towards spending, and later towards AI itself.
rows.settles: Tax systems unchanged as AI does a growing share of the work.
rows.who: This site, extending Anton Korinek and Lee M. Lockwood

rows.line: AI grows more unpopular even as more people use it, giving politicians on both the left and the right reason to campaign against it.
rows.settles: Public approval of AI rising clearly and politicians campaigning in its favour.

rows.line: In some quarter before 2034, output per person stands [test:bet_fast_side] or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before, which wins the bet's fast side.
rows.who: the fast side of the growth bet

rows.line: Firms using AI grow larger and take decisions further from the people on the spot.
rows.settles: Firms getting smaller and more decentralised as they adopt AI.

rows.line: The gap in value between versatile workers who manage AI and narrow specialists keeps widening.
rows.settles: Specialists keeping their value over versatile workers.

rows.line: Work in the jobs most exposed to AI grows more intense before it grows shorter.
rows.settles: Paid hours in the most exposed work falling before output per worker rises.

rows.line: Some jobs move from doing the work to supplying the data that trains AI to do it.
rows.settles: Few occupations showing workers shifting to producing training data.

rows.line: Labour's share of income falls as AI takes on more tasks, even as wages rise.
rows.settles: Labour's share holding while AI does a growing share of tasks.

rows.line: Cheap AI makes many small services worth selling that were never worth paying a person for, and filling these niches is how AI lifts growth.
rows.settles: New businesses in small information niches not rising as AI's costs fall.

rows.line: Care, teaching, hospitality and other work where the person is part of what is bought take a rising share of spending and jobs as AI spreads.
rows.settles: That work's share of spending and jobs falling as AI spreads.

rows.line: Law, contracting and other trades scattered by place stay split among many small firms, while the AI tools each trade uses gather around a few vendors.
rows.settles: A handful of labs ending up running, and profiting from, most professional work directly.

rows.line: Publishers lose the visits that pay for what they produce.
rows.settles: Visits to publishers from search and AI answers rising.

folios.label: Value capture
folios.question: Where do the profits end up?

rows.line: The AI 2027 scenario forecast that during 2025 AI company revenues would triple, yearly data-centre spending would double, and US AI power draw would grow by over five gigawatts.
Anthropic's revenue keeps growing about tenfold a year.
Leopold Aschenbrenner expected single companies such as Google or Microsoft to reach AI revenue of around a hundred billion dollars a year by about 2026.
Leopold Aschenbrenner projected that total annual AI investment could exceed a trillion dollars by 2027.
Daniel Kokotajlo foresaw that by 2026 AI assistants would be doing lucrative work across the economy, while world economic growth showed no visible acceleration yet.
Money is not what is scarce.
Firms' spending on AI per employee keeps rising, because what they use grows faster than the price of each unit falls.
rows.settles: Spending on AI per employee levelling off or falling while prices keep dropping.

rows.line: Buyers sign up for AI capacity well ahead of using it, so Microsoft's contracted but undelivered business keeps growing faster than its revenue.
rows.settles: The backlog shrinking against revenue; it is one company's figure and counts contracts of every kind, much of it OpenAI's commitment to Microsoft's cloud.

rows.line: Companies selling AI products keep lower gross margins than classic software, because every use costs them the model's price.
rows.settles: AI product margins reaching those of classic software.

rows.line: Profit moves up to the labs
rows.settles: The chip makers' hold on the profit loosens if, over a year, the labs' share of the gross profit we can measure rises by five points while the chip makers' share falls by as much.

rows.line: The biggest cloud and platform companies spend more each year on buildings and equipment than AI earns in revenue.
rows.settles: AI's revenue overtaking that spending.

rows.line: NVIDIA and AMD take more than [test:chips_collect] of the gross profit they share with Microsoft's cloud arm and the estimates for OpenAI and Anthropic.
rows.settles: Their share falling below that line while chips stay short.

rows.line: Open models trail the best closed ones by less than [test:gap_stays_short], a shorter gap than this site calls normal.
rows.settles: The best closed models pulling away from open ones by that gap or more.

rows.line: Open models carry most of the tokens routed to OpenRouter's busiest models.
rows.settles: The closed models' share of those tokens climbing back as the gap to open models closes.

rows.line: Users keep most of the value
rows.settles: Users rather than sellers keep most of the value if what people say they would need to be paid to give AI up is more than double the revenue the leading labs and business buyers bring in.

rows.line: AI earns trillions of dollars a year in revenue before 2030.
Leopold Aschenbrenner projected that the largest training cluster would draw about ten gigawatts and cost hundreds of billions of dollars by 2028.
Leopold Aschenbrenner projected a trillion-dollar training cluster by 2030, drawing about a hundred gigawatts, more than a fifth of current US electricity output.
AI needs about two trillion dollars of revenue a year by 2030 and falls short.
The gap between AI spending and the revenue to repay it keeps widening.
AI's revenue falls far short of what the spending on it needs to repay.
AI costs too much for the problems it can solve today.
Yafah Edelman and Anson Ho of Epoch AI argue that longer data-centre build times push the first trillion-dollar AI compute cluster from about 2030 back to about 2035.
The largest cloud companies spend many times more on AI buildings and chips than AI earns.
Advertising comes to pay for free AI assistants, because they can spot what people want to buy before search does, though keeping users' trust will be hard.
rows.settles: Ads in assistants driving users away or earning far less per user than ads in search.

rows.line: Apps that resell the labs' models see their margins shrink as their use grows.
rows.settles: A lab selling to apps below its public prices, or apps' margins holding as their use grows.

rows.line: NVIDIA's lead over other chip makers in sales for data centres keeps widening as AI spending grows.
rows.settles: Rival chip makers taking a growing share of data-centre chip sales while spending rises.

rows.line: NVIDIA keeps financing its own customers in return for a share of their income, and uses such deals to gain a say over who gets computing capacity.
rows.settles: NVIDIA's revenue staying almost wholly one-off sales of hardware.

rows.line: The cloud companies start storing new chips instead of installing them, the sign Cahn watches for that data centres are running late [cite:cahn_2025].
rows.settles: New chips going into service as fast as they arrive.

rows.line: The price of rented computing does not crash the way internet bandwidth did, because physical capacity cannot be multiplied overnight.
rows.settles: A sudden glut sending the rent for AI chips down by most of its value within a year.

rows.line: The market for training data stays split among many specialist sellers rather than gathering around one or two.
rows.settles: One or two sellers coming to handle most of what the frontier labs buy.

rows.line: Much of AI's everyday work moves out of distant data centres onto people's own phones and laptops.
rows.settles: Everyday use staying in cloud data centres as capable open models get smaller.

rows.line: Only a handful of labs stay at the frontier, because it costs too much capital for more.
rows.settles: More than a handful of labs keeping pace with the best models.

rows.line: The labs' margins are pulled down because the staff who deploy their models grow with their customers, which a pure software business avoids.
rows.settles: Labs reporting gross margins at or above classic software's while running large teams inside their customers.

rows.line: Being bought by a lab or a compute company becomes the usual way out for the start-ups that sell them data and tools.
rows.settles: The yearly count flattening, read only over quarters searched the same way. A later search that turns up deals missed earlier also raises the count, so it is not by itself a sign of more buying.

rows.line: Labs buy more of their training data straight from leading app companies and specialists, squeezing the firms that sell general practice environments.
rows.settles: General environment sellers keeping their share of the labs' data budgets.

rows.line: The leading labs may pull apart by industry, each strongest where it has bought the most specialist business records.
rows.settles: The labs staying interchangeable in every industry, with none ahead in a trade because of the data it bought.

rows.line: The lab with the best model keeps changing, because the leader uses its chips to serve its popular model while rivals train the next one.
rows.settles: One lab keeping the best model for several years running.

rows.line: Somewhere along the chip supply chain, a part AI has made scarce proves easier to expand than expected, and its price turns.
rows.settles: Every part squeezed by AI's demand staying scarce and rising in price.

rows.line: The labs earn a growing share of their revenue from products and deployments inside their customers' firms rather than from selling access to their models by the token.
rows.settles: The labs' revenue staying mostly in selling access to their models by the token.

rows.line: Labs' efforts to tie customers down, through exclusive deals and bans on copying their models, eventually fail, and moving between labs stays cheap.
rows.settles: Customers becoming bound to one lab by exclusive deals and bans on copying.

rows.line: Models keep differing in efficiency and in the kinds of input they handle, so they do not become an interchangeable utility like electricity.
rows.settles: Buyers treating models as interchangeable and choosing on the price of a token alone.

rows.line: Every firm ends up with a model of its own, trained on its own work.
rows.settles: Businesses' use of open models, the easiest kind to make one's own, falling further.

rows.line: Coding agents slow new firms' purchases of ready-made software but make the programs that hold a business's core records worth more.
rows.settles: Software that holds a business's records losing customers as fast as other software.

rows.line: The largest technology firms build more computing than they need and rent the spare to rivals, so the industry becomes one shared bet on demand for AI.
rows.settles: The largest firms keeping their computing for their own use and renting none of it out.

rows.line: Most businesses end up running models on machines they control rather than renting a lab's.
rows.settles: Businesses sticking with rented frontier models even as open models improve.

rows.line: Governments take direct stakes in the companies that make chips, power and models.
rows.settles: States staying lenders and buyers rather than owners.

rows.line: The people who use AI keep far more of its value than the firms that make it.
rows.settles: AI firms' profits growing as fast as the value their users get.

rows.line: Much narrow work AI does is turned into cheap fixed routines, so spending on each such task rises for a while and then stops.
rows.settles: Spending on well-defined tasks staying high after they are solved.

questions.question: Can models handle genuinely new problems?
Can they keep learning without forgetting?

questions.note: No public test measures it yet.
questions.question: Can they tell cause from coincidence?
Can they carry a long project through on their own?

questions.note: HAL, a Princeton benchmark, scores how predictable agents' failures are; this site stores it but does not draw it yet.
questions.question: Do they know when they are unsure?
Is AI speeding up its own research?

questions.note: Whether data made by machines keeps its quality has no public test.
questions.question: Will data and computing run short?

questions.note: HAL also scores consistency, robustness and safety; only accuracy and overall reliability are drawn.
questions.question: Are they reliable enough for work where mistakes are costly?

questions.note: No public test verifies a model's goals.
questions.question: Can we verify what they are aiming at?
Do bigger models still surprise us?

words.label: Happening
words.meaning: Tonight's reading is what the prediction says.

words.label: Not happening
words.meaning: Tonight's reading is against it, or its own test fails.

words.label: Slower than said
words.meaning: Moving the way it says, but behind the timetable it gave.

words.label: Both sides expect this
words.meaning: The reading fits this prediction and its rival alike, so it settles nothing yet.

words.label: Too early to tell
words.meaning: No reading can test it yet, the reading is too old, or its date has not come.
